The Moontail bullseye, Priacanthus hamrur, is a large-bodied priacanthid that attains a maximum fork length of 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters], a value documented from extensive trawl surveys across the Indo-Pacific region. This species exhibits a notably high asymptotic body mass, with the largest individuals reaching an ultimate wet weight of 1026 grams [Wwi = 1026 grams], a figure derived from length-weight regressions applied to adult specimens. In contrast, the size at which the onset of gonadal activity occurs is considerably smaller. Marked external sexual dimorphism is absent in this species, necessitating the use of histological examination of the gonads to pinpoint the timing of reproductive maturation. Field studies indicate that puberty is typically attained once fish cross a fork length of 22 centimeters [Lp = 22 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 130.6 grams [Wwp = 130.6 grams], a value calculated from species-specific length-weight regressions and consistent with the delayed maturation observed in many reef-associated predators. This relatively late onset of maturity relative to maximum size is a common life-history strategy among reef-associated predators, likely linked to the need to accumulate sufficient energy reserves before the first breeding cycle.

At a water temperature of 26.2 °C [T = 26.2 °C], ripe females were observed to produce approximately 672 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 672 eggs per spawning event], a count determined from oocyte size-frequency distributions. This moderate batch fecundity is offset by a very high spawning frequency, with individual females undertaking a single spawning event each day [F_R_i = single spawning event each day] over the protracted breeding season. This daily spawning rhythm, maintained at 26.2 °C, results in an exceptionally high reproductive output for a fish of its body size, reflecting the energetic advantages of inhabiting warm, productive tropical waters where planktonic larval food resources are abundant throughout much of the year.

Reproduction begins with the release of remarkably small pelagic eggs, whose size provides critical insight into the energetics of early life. Based on morphometric data from the congener Priacanthus macracanthus, the fertilized eggs of P. hamrur are estimated to measure 0.52 millimeters in diameter, yielding an initial wet weight at birth of just 0.000074 grams [Wwb = 0.000074 grams]. This extremely small size is typical of broadcast-spawning teleosts that produce a large number of tiny, yolk-poor eggs. The neonates pass through a very brief yolk-sac larva phase, with larval eclosion occurring within approximately 24 hours of external fertilization. The newly hatched, free-swimming larva is a transparent, planktonic organism that must immediately locate and capture its first prey, as the endogenous yolk reserves are exhausted within the first two days. Survival through this early larval bottleneck is largely dictated by the availability of appropriately sized copepod nauplii in the surrounding water column.

The lifespan and eventual senescence of the Moontail bullseye have been reconstructed from otolith annuli counts in populations from the western Indian Ocean. When exposed to a relatively stable thermal regime averaging 26.2 °C [T = 26.2 °C], the oldest recorded individual reached a lifespan of 3,650 days [am = 3,650 days], which represents approximately 10 years. This longevity is consistent with the species' moderate to slow life-history pace, characterized by delayed maturity and a low natural mortality rate once fish recruit to the adult reef habitat. There is no pronounced post-reproductive phase in this species; individuals remain reproductively active until the final year of life, with gonadal tissue showing progressive fibrosis and atretic degeneration only in the very oldest individuals. The species does not exhibit a single catastrophic, semelparous death; instead, mortality results from a combination of predation pressure on smaller adults and eventual physiological senescence in the largest, oldest fish.

Comparative trophic ecology offers additional context for the life-history traits of Priacanthus hamrur. As a nocturnal, zooplanktivorous predator, this species occupies a mid-level trophic position within reef food webs, consuming large quantities of copepods, decapod larvae, and small pelagic shrimps. The energetic surplus from this high-quality diet likely sustains the observed daily spawning rhythm and also underpins the species' ability to achieve a large ultimate wet weight of 1026 grams [Wwi = 1026 grams] despite the constraints of living in a structurally complex reef environment. Studies of its congener Priacanthus arenatus show a similar life-history syndrome, though P. hamrur attains a markedly larger size. The maximum recorded fork length of 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters] places it among the larger species within the Priacanthidae family, a position that may confer a reproductive advantage through increased fecundity and the ability to defend access to prime nocturnal foraging territories.
